children: ASML
says demand for its chipmaking equipment is now running so far ahead of planned production that the company expects
supply constraints to persist through at least 2028
The Dutch semiconductor-equipment giant said AI-related investment is driving stronger demand for advanced logic and memory chips, prompting customers to secure equipment years in advance.
Some customers are already expressing interest in placing orders for
, according to management.
ASML had already planned to increase capacity by roughly
30% in 2027 and another 30% in 2028
, but CEO Christophe Fouquet said those expansions will not be enough.

It is becoming very clear that 30% in 2027, 30% in 2028 will not allow us to meet our customer demand, Fouquet said. We have to do more, and we are looking basically at ways, especially in 2028 and beyond, to further extend our capacity.
That is a powerful demand signal for a company that already occupies one of the semiconductor industry's most critical bottlenecks.
ASML also raised its 2026 sales outlook.
The company now expects
44 billion to 45 billion in full-year net sales
, up from its previous range of 43 billion to 45 billion, with gross margin around 56%.
For the fourth quarter, ASML expects revenue of
14.2 billion to 15.2 billion
and gross margin around 57%.
Third-quarter sales came in at
11.7 billion
, with gross margin of 57.5% and net income of 4.96 billion.
Investor Takeaway
I think the most important part of ASML's update is not the guidance increase.
It is the fact that management is effectively saying
even aggressive capacity expansion is still falling short of customer demand
That tells investors two things.
First, AI infrastructure spending is translating into real equipment demand far down the semiconductor supply chain. Second, ASML's scarcity value remains extremely high.
For investors, the key metrics to watch are
order intake, backlog, capacity expansion, gross margins and whether customers continue placing orders several years in advance
The main risk is execution. Expanding capacity faster could pressure costs or create oversupply later if AI spending slows.
But for now, the message from ASML is unusually clear: demand is not the problem. Producing enough equipment is.

title: ASML Sounds Alarm as 30% Capacity Boost Falls Short
